Nonetheless, the magnitude of initial Spike-specific T cell IFN-γ response may only partially predict the durability and polyfunctionality of T cell memory. Additional signs of a robust spike-reactive clonal diversity, captured by TCR sequencing, could encompass a wider range of receptor affinities beneficial for T cell survival in germinal centers or sustained tissue-resident immunity, consistent with a prior study showing that SARS-CoV-2 T cell clonal diversity, rather than individual clonotype abundance in blood, better predicted persistence of cellular memory 40.

The primary study population in the COV-BOOST trial was drawn from multiple sites in the United Kingdom, enriched for so far well studied HLA alleles (e.g., A*02:01, A*03:01, B*08:01), which increases the chance that the SARS-CoV-2 S reactive catalog developed in this study matched vaccine elicited receptors. Although this cohort was not large enough to definitively assess whether risk of symptomatic breakthrough infection varied due to carriership of single HLA variants, it was notable that fewer symptomatic infections were observed in individuals carrying HLA-A*03:01, the second best represented class I allele in the newly developed HLA SARS-CoV-2 S catalog, with over 400 reference receptors. The robust contribution of A*03:01-linked receptors to E[HA-T S ] breadth is consistent with the hypothesis that specific HLA alleles that activate diverse vaccine acquired CD8 + T cells may enhance effective immunological control [40] [41] [42] . Other recent studies have shown A*03:01 carriership may be associated with improved humoral response to vaccination 43 , reduced risk of breakthrough infections 44 and lower rate of long COVID-19 45 . We also observed that fewer symptomatic infections occurred in participants with the HLA-DQA*0102/HLA-DQB*0602 haplotype, which was also well represented in the newly developed SARS-CoV-2 catalog. The HLA-DQB1*06 allele has been previously linked to robust antibody responses against the Spike RBD after vaccination in the COV001 and COV002 trials, and HLA-DQB1*06 carriership was previously associated with lower risk of breakthrough infection after primary vaccination in a UK based study population 46.

The methodology employed in this study to generate an HLA-linked SARS-CoV-2 spike catalog integrated data from multiple data sets benefited from unprecedented immunological data collection that occurred during the SAR-CoV-2 pandemic. In order to generate similarly effective reference sets for other respiratory pathogens (e.g., Influenza, RSV, or Mycobacterium tuberculosis ) it is likely that large scale data collection and sharing are needed to provide the foundation for robust and portable TCRseq-based biomarker development. Recently developed tools for HLA imputation directly from TCR repertoire data 24, 47, 48 and exposure-linked TCR clustering graph algorithms 49, 50 can facilitate the fusion of HLA-labeled and unlabeled data and can help derive TCR-HLA-immunogen associations needed to denoise partial information contained in single chain TCR sequences 51 and uncover blood based signals of cellular mediated immunity that could improve durability and population coverage of future vaccines. or BioNTech BNT162b2 (BNT) at least 84 days prior to the time of enrolment 19, 20 . In this study participant samples were considered if they received one of the following booster vaccines: AstraZeneca ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (ChAd), Janssen Ad26. COV2. S (Ad26), mRNA BioNTech BNT162b2 (BNT), mRNA Moderna mRNA-1273 (MOD), or protein subunit Novavax NVX-CoV2373 (NVX). Based on sample availability, we analyzed a set of participants with paired Day 0 and Day 14 PBMC samples for TCR sequencing and functional assays. Cases were determined by a positive SARS-CoV-2 test (e.g.,an antigen detection or nucleic acid amplification test) starting 1 week after vaccination. Non-case controls were participants with no evidence of symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection through the end of April 2022.

Based on sample availability, controls were selected from eligible non-cases in proportion to the treatment assignment of the cases. From available samples, one male and one female non-case participant of similar age was selected for every case. After sample processing, the final dataset comprised 120 participants (43 cases and 77 controls) with matched Day 0 and Day 14 TCR repertoires. Participant HLA information was not considered in sample selection.

Construction of an HLA-linked SARS-CoV-2 Spike-reactive TCR Catalog

To construct a large catalog of HLA-linked SARS-CoV-2 Spike-reactive T cell receptors (TCRs), we integrated prior public data. We considered evidence from cohort-wide statistical enrichment testing, longitudinal vaccination studies, and previously published experimental validation datasets. Our objective was to maximize sensitivity for identifying candidate Spike-reactive clonotypes from bulk single-chain TCRβ data while preserving information regarding the strength evidence for TCRβ-antigen-specificity through sequence-level confidence weighting.

HLA-linked SARS-CoV-2-associated TCRs

To identify novel HLA-associated TCRs induced by SARS-CoV-2 infection, we analyzed 1,355 TCR repertoires previously collected from individuals with acute and convalescent COVID-19 23, 52 . As HLA genotypes were not available for these repertoires, common HLA alleles were imputed directly from the TCR repertoire features using previously described methods for high-confidence HLA genotype inference with TCR2HLA 24.

We then evaluated public TCRs within these post-infection repertoires for associations with individual HLA alleles. Each TCRβ receptor was represented by its TRBV-gene family (e.g., V05, V01) and its complete CDR3β amino acid (AA) sequences. For each common imputable allele (e.g. A*01:01) or haplotype (e.g. DQA1*05:01/DQB1*02:01), we tested whether a given TCRβ or its edit-1 AA mutational variant was enriched among carriers relative to non-carriers. This analysis identified numerous HLA-associated TCRs that were distinct from previously identified HLA-linked reference receptorslikely associated with other common viral exposures 24 -yielding a catalog of putative SARS-CoV-2-associated clonotypes linked to specific HLA alleles. If a receptor sequence (TRBV-family-CDR3(AA) was strongly linked to multiple alleles or haplotypes, we retained all possible associations for downstream detection.

Identification of Putative SARS-CoV-2-Spike-reactive Clonotypes

Because the post-infection repertoires contained TCRs targeting multiple SARS-CoV-2 antigens, including likely immunodominant responses against the nucleocapsid and ORF1 proteins, we next sought to identify receptors likely reactive to the S protein found in current vaccines. Candidate HLA-linked TCRs were evaluated using paired pre-and post-vaccination repertoires from three previously published cohorts of mRNA vaccine recipients 26, 41, 42 , the COV-BOOST cohort, and a separate COV002 cohort.

Post-vaccine samples were only considered if they were collected within 7-45 days after two-dose primary or booster vaccination.

For each candidate TCR, we assessed enrichment among individuals carrying the predicted HLA-allele following vaccination. A sequence was retained as putatively Spike-reactive if it was detected more frequently in HLA-matched post-vs. pre-vaccination repertoires. Because relatively few vaccinated participants possessed each inferred HLA allele, we intentionally applied permissive enrichment criteria to maximize sensitivity and retain potentially informative sequences (odds ratio > 1; Fisher's exact test p < 0.5).

Assignment of TCRβ-level Confidence Weights

To estimate the strength of evidence supporting each putative Spike-reactive TCR, we compared the frequency of each candidate clonotype between HLA-matched post-vaccination repertoires and pre-2019 SARS-CoV-2-naïve repertoires.Sequences with odds ratios greater than one were retained. We then transformed odds ratios using Yule's Q statistic: , 𝑄 = ( 𝑂𝑅 -1 ) / ( 𝑂𝑅 + 1 ) which bounds enrichment estimates between 0 and 1. The resulting Q value was assigned as a sequence-level confidence weight, with larger values, closer to 1, indicating stronger enrichment in post-vaccination repertoires and therefore greater confidence that the detection of that TCRβ clonotype represents S antigen recognition as opposed to sampling noise or an irrelevant TCRα:TCRβ pairing.

Experimentally Validated Spike-reactive TCRs

To augment the catalog of statistically inferred clonotypes, we incorporated TCR sequences supported by direct experimental evidence of peptide-HLA binding. We curated Spike-reactive clonotypes identified through tetramer or multimer staining assays from previously published studies 41, [53] [54] [55] [56] [57] [58] [59] . In addition, we included previously reported HLA-A*03:01-associated Spike-reactive clonotypes identified by activation inducible marker-TCRseq validation through cluster-representative Jurkat peptide stimulation assays 41 . These experimentally supported sequences were filtered and assigned confidence weights using the same bounded Yule's Q transformation framework described above.

Vaccine-responsive HLA-linked Clonotypes

We additionally used longitudinal vaccination studies to identify clonotypes exhibiting evidence of vaccine-induced expansion. Using paired pre-and post-vaccination repertoires from prior studies 26, 41, 42 , we quantified clonal expansion of individual TCRs following mRNA vaccination. Clonotypes were retained if they demonstrated both substantial expansion (fold change > 2) and statistical significant change in template counts (FDR-adjusted Fisher's exact test p < 0.05). To link these expansions to HLA-restricted responses, expanded clonotypes were only retained receptors if they could be assigned to a common HLA allele or haplotype through enrichment testing in the post-infection repertoires (p < 0.01).

Confidence weights for kinetically identified clonotypes were assigned using the same Yule's Q-based framework described above.

Construction of the Final HLA-linked Spike-reactive TCR Catalog

Thus, the final catalog was assembled by combining evidence from three complementary sources: (i) statistically inferred HLA-linked Spike-reactive clonotypes, (ii) experimentally validated Spike-reactive TCRs, and (iii) vaccine-responsive clonotypes identified through prior longitudinal repertoire analysis.

When a clonotype was supported by multiple methods, redundant clones were collapsed into a single record linked to the corresponding HLA allele or haplotype. The resulting catalog contains 7,163 HLA-linked Spike-reactive TCRs annotated with sequence-level confidence weights, which we used to quantify HLA-aware Spike-specific T cell breadth.

HLA-aware Spike-specific T Cell Breadth (HA-T S Breadth) metric

Antigen specific breadth is a commonly used metric in TCR sequencing analysis to describe the clonotypic diversity of a T cell recognizing an antigen. It is the proportion of clonotypes matching a reference catalog divided by the total unique receptor sequence in the sample. We developed an HLA-aware measure of T cell breadth based on the catalog of HLA-linked Spike-reactive TCRs described above. Unlike conventional breadth metrics that count all diagnostic SARS-CoV-2-reactive clonotypes equally, this approach restricted breadth estimate to only clonotypes linked to HLA alleles carried by the participant and incorporated sequence-level confidence weights (described above).

For each participant, genotyped HLA alleles were compared against the HLA-linked Spike-reactive TCR catalog. Catalog entries corresponding to at least one of the participant's HLA alleles were considered eligible matches. Participant repertoires were then screened for the presence of eligible catalog clonotypes. Each matched clonotype contributed a sequence-level confidence weight, reflecting the strength of statistical or experimental evidence supporting its Spike specificity. HLA-aware Spike-specific T cell breadth for participant was calculated as:

For participant j, N j is the number of total unique clones in the post-vaccine repertoire sample. U is the set of all antigen-associated TCRs in the HLA-CoV2S-TCRβ catalog , and U Hj denotes the subset associated with the HLA alleles expressed by participant j.

Estimation of Expected HLA-intrinsic Breadth

To separate the contribution of HLA genotype from realized T cell responses, we estimated an expected HLA-intrinsic breadth (E[T S, HLA ]), using only each participant's HLA genotype. Using an independent cohort of mRNA-vaccinated individuals 26 , we constructed allele-specific breadth distributions and performed Monte Carlo sampling across the class I and class II alleles carried by each participant to generate a genotype-specific distribution of expected breadth values (Extended Data Fig. 8 ).

The median of each participant's sampled distribution was used as the participant's expected

HLA-intrinsic breadth estimates (E[HA-T S ]).

We additionally calculated two normalized measures of repertoire performance relative to this genetic baseline. The residual breadth ratio, R(HA-T S ) = HA-T S / (E[HA-T S ]), which quantifies observed breadth relative to genotype-derived expectation. We also calculated a breadth quantile score, Q(HA-T S ) defined as the percentile rank of the observed breadth within the participant's simulated genotype-specific breadth distribution. These metrics were subsequently evaluated as predictors of infection risk. We compared levels of E[HA-T S, HLA ], R(HA-T S Q), and Q(HA-T S ) between cases and controls to assess whether infection risk was associated with HLA-intrinsic breadth potential, repertoire performance relative to genetic expectation, or both.

HLA-Genotyping

TCR Sequencing of COV-BOOST Samples

For the COV-BOOST study, genomic DNA was isolated (as described for HLA-genotyping) from four million, T-cell Xtend (Catalog number: TTK610, Oxford Immunotec, Abingdon, UK) isolated PBMCs, sourced from whole blood samples (Southampton, UK). Multiplex PCR amplification and high-throughput sequencing of TRBV gene segments and CDR3β regions of the human T-cell receptor β (TCRβ) locus were performed using the standard ImmunoSEQ protocol (Adaptive Biotechnologies, Seattle, WA). Six participants were excluded from downstream analysis because their sample sets possessed insufficient starting DNA material (flagged by Adaptive Biotechnologies' laboratory) or lacked minimal clonal overlap between timepoints, suggesting a sample labeling error. To reduce variability due to differences in DNA extraction yield and sequencing depth, TCR repertoires were resampled with replacement to a uniform depth of 100,000 templates per sample prior to downstream analyses.

Previously Developed TCR-based SARS-CoV-2 S Metrics

To compare among HLA-aware Spike-specific breadth and previously established HLA-agnostics approaches, we calculated several published SARS-CoV-2-specific TCR sequencing metrics from each repertoire. These included Adaptive Biotechnologies' proprietary Spike breadth metric, MIRA-derived SARS-CoV-2 breadth, and the Spike V3 classifier score 21, 22.

The Spike breadth metric was defined as the proportion of unique TCR clonotypes matching previously

Interferon-γ ELISpot

For cellular immunology readouts, PBMC samples were collected from nine sites based on logistical reasons (i.e. proximity to the external laboratory). Interferon-γ (IFN-γ)-secreting T cells were quantified by stimulating PBMCs from study participants with 15-mer peptides spanning the Wuhan-Hu-1 protein sequence (YP_009724390.1), with an 11-amino-acid overlap between consecutive peptides. IFN-γ-secreting T cells were detected using a modified T-SPOT Discovery assay (Oxford Immunotec, Abingdon, UK). Samples were processed within 32 hours of venepuncture, with the T-Cell Xtend reagent added to remove red blood cells, and granulocytes and extend PBMC viability during sample processing. T-cell responses were reported as spot-forming cells (SFCs) per 250,000 PBMCs. The lower limit of detection was 1 SFC per 250,000 PBMCs.

Results were multiplied by four to express T-cell frequencies as SFCs per 1 × 10 6 PBMCs. Extended Data Fig 1: Diverse HLA-associated TCR features are represented in the SARS-CoV-2 catalog.

Cohort and Participant SelectionCOV-BOOST was a multicentre, randomised, phase 2 trial evaluating third-dose booster vaccination against COVID-19, with a prespecified subgroup undergoing detailed immunological assessments. We utilized samples collected as part of this trial which was conducted at 18 sites across the UK, encompassing both community and secondary-care settings. The trial was reviewed and approved by the South Central-Berkshire Research Ethics Committee and the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency. The trial was registered with EudraCT (2021-002175-19) and the Integrated Research Application System (IRAS 299180; REC reference 21/SC/0171). Participants had previously received two doses of either AstraZeneca ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 (ChAd) symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection were evaluated using a calendar-stratified Cox proportional hazards model to account June and November vaccination start months.

Inverse probability weights (IPW) were applied based on case status and vaccine platform to account for the two phase case-control sampling design and recover population-level hazard estimates. For IPW weighting, participants were grouped by general prime-boost vaccine modalities: (i) Adenovirus / Adenovirus, (ii) . mRNA / mRNA, (ii) Adenovirus / mRNA, (iv) mRNA / Adenovirus, (v) . Adenovirus / Protein Subunit, (vi) mRNA / Protein Subunit. The primary endpoint was time to symptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection, defined according to the COV-BOOST trial protocol as home antigen test-or PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection accompanied by compatible symptoms. Follow-up time was calculated from the date of immunologic sampling until the first documented symptomatic infection or censoring. The primary immunologic variable was HLA-aware Spike-specific T cell breadth (HA-T S ). Hazard ratios (HRs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals were estimated using IPW stratified Cox proportional hazards regression. To evaluate the relative and independent contributions of cellular and humoral immunity, we compared models incorporating HA-T S Breadth, pseudovirus neutralization assay (PNA) neutralization titer 50 (NT50), and IFN-γ ELISpot responses measured at Day 14. NT50 represents potential antibody-mediated protection, whereas HA-T S Breadth and ELISpot capture complementary aspects of cellular immunity, By comparing nested models containing individual and combined immune correlates, we evaluated whether associations between HLA-aware T cell breadth and infection risk persisted after accounting for humoral immunity and conventional functional T cell response magnitude. Analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.3 using the survival package (version 3.8).

Three sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the influence of these samples on the estimated association between HA-TS breadth and risk of symptomatic breakthrough infection: Low-recovery samples were excluded and the primary Cox model refit in the remaining 98 participants (Extended Data Fig 5 C,D model 2), Imputation of low-recovery values. All participants were retained and Day 14 HA-T S breadth was imputed for low-recovery samples. A linear regression of Day 14 on Day 0 log2(HA-T S ) breadth was fit in the 98 samples with at least 100,000 productive templates, excluding two near-zero Day 0 breadth values, and used to predict Day 14 values for the low-recovery samples (Extended Data Fig 5 F, G). Observed values were retained for all other participants. Imputation was supported by a positive correlation between timepoints in the retained samples (Pearson r = 0.58, p < 0.0001). Each of the three model sets was refit with an additional covariate for inverse repertoire richness, log2(1/R), where R is the number of unique TCRs recovered after downsampling (Extended Data Fig 5 models 1A, 2A, 3A), and separately with log2(NT50) (Extended Data Fig 5 models 1B, 2B, 3B). All models were stratified, inverse-probability-weighted Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for age and sex, matching the specification of the primary analysis.

Genomic

DNA was extracted from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) samples collected at Day 0, Day 14, or Day 28 post vaccination from each unique study participant. DNA extractions were carried out using the QIAamp DNA Blood Mini Kit (Cat. No. 51106; QIAGEN, Venlo, The Netherlands), according to the manufacturer's instructions. Samples yielding >3.5 µg of total DNA at a concentration of >100 ng/µL were submitted to Histogenetics (Ossining, NY, USA) for HLA genotyping. Prior to sequencing, DNA samples underwent quality control assessment. HLA genotyping was performed using Illumina MiSeq/NovaSeq sequencing to characterize the HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C, HLA-DRB1, HLA-DRB3/DRB4/DRB5 (DRB345), HLA-DQB1, HLA-DQA1, HLA-DPB1, and HLA-DPA1 loci at 1X high-resolution level.

identified Spike-associated public TCR sequences.The Spike V3 score represents a logistic regression based classifier-derived measure based on Spike TCRs predictive of SARS-COV-2 exposure. MIRA breadth was calculated using experimentally mapped SARS-CoV-2-reactive TCRs identified through Multiplex Identification of T-cell Receptor Antigen Specificity (MIRA) assays 23 but not necessarily part of the diagnostic set of enhanced sequences 21 . All metrics were evaluated alongside HLA-aware Spike-specific breadth in case vs non-case comparisons. Previously developed adaptive SARS-CoV-2 S TCR metrics were computed on the exact same resampled repertoires as were used in the primary analysis.
